questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution mentioned that the Prime Minister is appointed by the President of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer __Article 75__. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Article 75–Other Provisions as to Ministers

 
 
• ​**The Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President** and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
 
• The total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Council of Ministers, shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. This provision was added by the 91st Amendment Act of 2003.
 
• A member of either house of Parliament belonging to any political party who is disqualified on the ground of defection shall also be disqualified to be appointed as a minister. This provision was also added by the 91st Amendment Act of 2003.
 
• The ministers shall hold office during the pleasure of the President.
 
• The council of ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
 
• The President shall administer the oaths of office and secrecy to a minister.
 
• A minister who is not a member of the Parliament (either house) for any period of six consecutive months shall cease to be a minister.
 
• The salaries and allowances of ministers shall be determined by the Parliament.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__** 

__
 
• RESPONSIBILITY OF MINISTERS

 
 
• Collective Responsibility

 
 
• The fundamental principle underlying the working of the parliamentary system of government is the principle of collective responsibility.
 
• Article 75 clearly states that the council of ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
 
• This means that all the ministers own joint responsibility to the Lok Sabha for all their acts of omission and commission.
 
• They work as a team and swim or sink together.
 
• When the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against the council of ministers, all the ministers have to resign including those ministers who are from the Rajya Sabha.
 
• The principle of collective responsibility also means that the Cabinet decisions bind all cabinet ministers (and other ministers) even if they differed in the cabinet meeting. 
 
• It is the duty of every minister to stand by cabinet decisions and support them both within and outside the Parliament.
 
• If any minister disagrees with a cabinet decision and is not prepared to defend it, he must resign.
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• Individual Responsibility

 
 
• Article 75 also contains the principle of individual responsibility.
 
• It states that the ministers hold office during the pleasure of the president, which means that the President can remove a minister even at a time when the council of ministers enjoys the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
 
• However, the President removes a minister only on the advice of the Prime Minister.

questions.question: Which of the following articles guarantees that no person shall be punished on the basis of laws enacted after a crime has been committed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 20. **__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• Article 20 of the Constitution of India deals with the protection of certain rights in case of conviction for offenses.
 
• It provides safeguards for persons who have been accused of committing a crime and are facing trial or have been convicted.
 
• The article consists of three clauses, which are:
 
 
• Protection against ex-post facto laws: This clause prohibits the government from passing any law that punishes a person for an act that was not an offense when it was committed. **Hence, the correct answer is Option 3.**
 
• In other words, a person cannot be punished for an act that was legal at the time it was committed but later became an offense.
 
• Protection against double jeopardy: This clause states that no person can be prosecuted or punished for the same offense more than once.
 
• Protection against self-incrimination: This clause provides that no person accused of an offense shall be compelled to be a witness against himself/herself.
 
 
 
• These three clauses are fundamental protections for the rights of the accused, and they are intended to ensure that individuals are not subjected to unjust or arbitrary treatment by the state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• The protection of life and personal liberty is guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

 
 
• This article states that "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law."
 
• The Supreme Court of India has interpreted this article in a broad and expansive manner to include within its ambit a wide range of rights and freedoms, such as the right to privacy, the right to live with dignity, and the right to a fair trial.
 
• The protection of life and personal liberty is considered to be one of the most fundamental and important rights guaranteed by the Constitution, and it is an essential component of a democratic and just society.
 
 
 
• The abolition of untouchability is guaranteed under Article 17 of the Constitution of India.
 
 
• This article states that "Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of Untouchability shall be an offense punishable in accordance with the law."
 
• The practice of untouchability, which involves the exclusion and segregation of individuals based on their caste, is considered to be a social evil and a violation of human rights.
 
• The Constitution of India recognizes the importance of abolishing untouchability and ensures that any form of discrimination or prejudice based on caste is prohibited and punishable by law.
 
 
 
• The right to education is guaranteed under Article 21A of the Constitution of India, which was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act in 2002.
 
• This article states that "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine."
 
• The right to education is considered to be a fundamental right and an essential component of a democratic and just society.
 
• The Constitution of India recognizes the importance of providing access to education for all children, and it places the responsibility on the State to ensure that every child between the ages of six and fourteen has access to free and compulsory education.

• Ammonium iron(II) sulphate(Mohr's salt) is an inorganic compound that chemical formula is **FeSO4. (NH4)2SO4.6H2****O** or (NH4)2Fe(SO4)2(H2O)6.

• Mohr's salt is named after Karl Friedrich Mohr, a German chemist.
 
• Mohr salt is prepared by dissolving, in water containing a small amount of sulfuric acid, an equimolar mixture of hydrated ferrous sulphate and ammonium sulphate, and then by crystallising the resulting solution.
 
• Light green crystals are formed by ferrous ammonium sulphate. As heated, this salt ionises to deliver all the cations and anions present in it.

questions.question: Identify the INCORRECT statement about fermentation.

options.text: Fermentation occurs only in fungal cells.
The fermentation technique is used to make breads.
It is the process of breaking down sugar into alcohol.
Yeast is used in fermentation technology to prepare alcohol.

questions.solution:

__
 
• Fermentation is the process by which molecules such as glucose are broken down anaerobically.
 
• **Many bacteria and yeasts** carry out fermentation. People use these organisms to make **yogurt, bread, wine, and biofuels**.** Human muscle cells also use fermentation**. This occurs when muscle cells cannot get oxygen fast enough to meet their energy needs through aerobic respiration. **Hence, it is incorrect to say that fermentation occurs only in fungal cells.**
 
• The fermentation technique is used to** make breads.**
 
• By the process of fermentation, the sugars are converted into alcohol.__
 
• The enzymes like pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase catalyze these reactions.
 
• It normally occurs in__ yeast cells bacteria__ and in the muscles of animals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• Fermentation is a method of extracting energy from molecules.
 
• Fermentation accounts for only a partial breakdown of glucose.
 
• In fermentation, there is a net gain of only two molecules of ATP for each molecule of glucose degraded to pyruvic acid.
 
• Wine and beer are produced by fermentation.
 
• No ATP would be produced without fermentation.

questions.question: Which are the two most common minerals found in rocks?
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is 'Feldspar and quartz'**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• **Feldspar and quartz:**

 
 
• Feldspar and quartz are the two most common minerals found in the Earth's crust.
 
• Feldspar comprises a group of minerals that are abundant, accounting for about 60% of the Earth's crust. It includes a variety of compositions such as potassium feldspar and plagioclase feldspar.
 
• Quartz is a silica mineral and makes up about 12% of the Earth's crust. It is known for its hardness and resistance to weathering.
 
• Both minerals are important components of granite, the most common continental rock, and are also found in many other igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bauxite and Calcite:**

 
 
• Bauxite is not a mineral but a rock composed of aluminum-bearing minerals like gibbsite, boehmite, and diaspore. It is the principal ore of aluminum but not common as a primary mineral in most rocks.
 
• Calcite is common, particularly in sedimentary rocks like limestone and marble, but it is not as prevalent in the Earth's crust as feldspar and quartz.
 
 
 
• **Mica and Calcite:**
 
 
• Mica encompasses a group of phyllosilicate minerals that form in sheets or layers. It is commonly found in igneous and metamorphic rocks, but not as widespread as feldspar.
 
• Similarly, while calcite is significant in sedimentary environments, it does not contribute as extensively to the Earth's crust composition as feldspar and quartz.
 
 
 
• **Amphibole and Olivine:**
 
 
• Amphiboles are a group of silicate minerals typically found in metamorphic rocks like schists, as well as in some igneous rocks.
 
• Olivine is a mineral commonly found in mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks, such as basalt and peridotite. While important, these minerals are less abundant in the crust compared to feldspar and quartz.

• Near the city of Sambalpur, a large dam - the Hirakud Dam - is built on the river.

Godavari river

 
• Godavari river with the second-longest course within India, Godavari is often referred to as the Vriddh (Old) Ganga or the Dakshin (South) Ganga.
 
• The river is about 1,450 km (900 miles) long.
 
• It rises at Trimbakeshwar, near Nasik and Mumbai in Maharashtra around 380 km distance from the Arabian Sea, but flows southeast across south-central India through the states of Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Orissa, and Andhra Pradesh, and empties into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• Some of its tributaries include Indravati River, Pranahita (Combination of Penuganga and Warda), Manjira, Bindusara and Sabari.
 
• Some important urban centers on its banks include Nasik, Bhadrachalam, Rajahmundry, and Narsapur.

Krishna River

 
• The Krishna is one of the longest rivers of India (about 1300 km in length).
 
• It originates at Mahabaleswar in Maharashtra, passes through Sangli, and meets the sea in the Bay of Bengal at Hamasaladeevi in Andhra Pradesh.
 
• The Krishna River flows through the states of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh.
 
• Its most important tributary is the Tungabhadra River, which itself is formed by the Tunga and Bhadra rivers that originate in the Western Ghats.
 
• Other tributaries include the Koyna, Bhima, Mallaprabha, Ghataprabha, Yerla, Warna, Dindi, Musi, and Dudhganga rivers.

Kaveri River

 
• The Kaveri (also spelled Cauvery or Kavery) is one of the great rivers of India and is considered sacred by the Hindus.
 
• The headwaters are in the Western Ghats range of Karnataka state, and from Karnataka through Tamil Nadu.
 
• It empties into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• The source of the river is Talakaveri located in the Western Ghats about 5,000 feet (1,500 m) above sea level.
 
• It has many tributaries including Shimsha, Hemavati, Arkavathy, Kapila, Honnuhole, Lakshmana Tirtha, Kabini, Lokapavani, Bhavani, Noyyal, and Famous Amaravati.

questions.question: According to __________________ of the Constitution of India, no person shall be compelled to pay any taxes for the promotion of a particular religion.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 27.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• Article 27:- Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion.

 
 
• No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically appropriated in payment of expenses for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• Article 25 to 28 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Right to Freedom of Religion. 
 
• Article 25:- Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion. 
 
 
• Subject to public order, morality, and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practice, and propagate religion.
 
• Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from making any law:-
 
 
• Regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political, or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice.
 
• Providing for social welfare and reform or the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.
 
 
 
 
 
• Article 26:- Freedom to manage religious affairs.
 
 
• Subject to public order, morality, and health, every religious denomination or any section thereof shall have the right:-
 
 
• To establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes. 
 
• To manage its own affairs in matters of religion. 
 
• To own and acquire movable and immovable property. 
 
• To administer such property in accordance with the law.
 
 
 
 
 
• 
 
• Article 28:- Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions.

 
• No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds.
 
• Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to an educational institution that is administered by the State but has been established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution.
 
• No person attending any educational institution recognized by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction that may be imparted in such institution or to attend any religious worship that may be conducted in such institution or in any premises attached thereto unless such person or, if such person is a minor, his guardian has given his consent thereto.

questions.question: India’s drainage system is divided on the basis of the size of the watershed. Which of the following is NOT a part of the drainage basin of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Average** **river** **basin**. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• India's drainage system is primarily divided on the basis of the size of the watershed.
 
• The two main categories are major river basins and their tributaries.
 
• **Major** **river** **basin**:
 
 
• This is a valid classification. Major river basins include the large river systems in India, such as the Ganges, Brahmaputra, Yamuna, Godavari, Krishna, and others.
 
• These rivers play a crucial role in India's geography and water management.
 
 
 
• **Minor** **river** **basin**:
 
 
• This is a valid classification as well. Minor river basins refer to the tributaries and smaller river systems that contribute to the major rivers.
 
• They are essential for the overall drainage network.
 
 
 
• **Average** **river** **basin**:
 
 
• This term is not a standard classification in the context of India's drainage system.
 
• The classification is typically based on the size and importance of the rivers and their basins. "Average river basin" is not a recognized category. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

Detailed Information about Indian Drainage System:

 
• **Himalayan Rivers**:

 
 
• The Himalayan rivers, including the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and their tributaries, are crucial components of India's drainage system.
 
• These rivers originate in the Himalayas and contribute significantly to the country's water resources.
 
 
 
• **Peninsular Rivers:**
 
 
• The peninsular rivers, such as the Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, and others, flow through the Peninsular region.
 
• They play a vital role in irrigation and are important for agriculture.
 
 

Drainage Patterns in India:

 
• **Dendritic Pattern**:

 
 
• The dendritic pattern is common in areas with uniform geological structure.
 
• The rivers resemble the branches of a tree, and it is prevalent in the Peninsular region.
 
 
 
• **Trellis Pattern**:
 
 
• This pattern is characterized by the main rivers and their tributaries flowing parallel to each other.
 
• It is common in regions with alternating layers of hard and soft rocks.
 
 
 
• **Radial Pattern:**
 
 
• Radial drainage pattern is observed when rivers flow outward from a central high point, like spokes on a wheel.
 
• This pattern is common around volcanic cones.
 
 
 
• **Rectangular Pattern**:
 
 
• Rectangular drainage pattern occurs when rivers follow the joint and fault lines in the terrain, creating a grid-like pattern.
